```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

This tutorial follows a small survey from inspection to tabulation, grouped
summaries and new variables. Results are ordinary R objects that you can save,
filter and join. Install tidystata as shown on the
[package homepage](https://socimh.github.io/tidystata/) before starting.

## Load data and inspect variables

```{r data}
library(tidystata)
library(dplyr)

survey <- tibble(
  id = 1:6,
  group = c("A", "A", "A", "B", "B", NA),
  response = c("yes", "no", NA, "yes", "yes", "no"),
  score1 = c(2, 4, NA, 6, 8, 10),
  score2 = c(4, NA, NA, 8, 10, 12)
)
attr(survey$score1, "label") <- "First assessment score"

codebook(survey)
variables(survey)
ds(survey, starts_with("score"))
```

`codebook()` gives one row per variable. `variables()` reports names and variable
labels, while `ds()` returns a character vector of names. `variables_search()`
searches names and labels, so it can find a variable from its description:

```{r select}
variables_search(survey, "assessment")
select_or_transmute(survey, id, starts_with("score"))
```

## Count categories

```{r count}
counts <- tab(survey, response)
counts
sum(counts$n)

fre(survey, response)
tab2(survey, group, response)
```

The counts sum to six, including the missing response. `tab()` returns observed
categories with counts and percentages. `fre()` adds total rows; `tab2()` puts
the categories of its second variable into columns. Use `tab1()` when you want
separate one-way tables instead of a joint table:

```{r count-list}
tables <- tab1(survey, group, response)
tables$response
```

The returned objects contain data. For example, select categories occurring
more than once with an ordinary pipeline:

```{r count-pipeline}
tab(survey, response) |>
  filter(n > 1)
```

## Summarise measurements

Select numeric measurements deliberately. Codes attached to categories are not
automatically meaningful measurements.

```{r summary}
summ(survey, score1, score2, .stat = c("n", "mean", "sd", "missing"))
tabstat(survey, score1, score2, .by = group)
mean(survey$score1, na.rm = TRUE)
```

`summ()` can return several statistics. `tabstat()` selects means by default.
Both omit missing measured values from numeric calculations. Missing grouping
keys remain as a group unless you request `.missing = FALSE`:

```{r groups}
summ(survey, score1, .by = group, .missing = FALSE, .stat = c("n", "mean"))
```

Numeric-only summaries return a table. When numeric and calendar measurements
are combined, the default can be a list of tables. The companion
`vignette("containers-and-missing-values", package = "tidystata")` explains those
types and their missing-value conventions.

## Prepare new variables

Row helpers return vectors, making them convenient in `mutate()`. `pick()` makes
the columns being combined explicit.

```{r rows}
prepared <- survey |>
  mutate(
    average = row_mean(pick(score1, score2)),
    observed = row_non_miss(pick(score1, score2))
  )
prepared
```

The third row has no observed score, so its average is `NA` and its observed
count is zero. Row sums use zero for an all-missing row, while column summaries
use `NA` for a sum with no observations.

Character measurements can be parsed explicitly, and sentinel values can be
replaced before calculations:

```{r conversion}
destring(c("1,200", "2,500", NA))
mvdecode(c(1, -99, 3), -99)
xtile(1:8, 4)
stata_recode(c(2, 4.5, 7, 12), 1:5 ~ 1, 6:10 ~ 2)
```

`destring()` reads numbers with currency symbols, thousands separators and
percent signs; other text, such as `"10 kg"`, becomes `NA` with a warning
unless you remove it with `ignore = "kg"`. `xtile()` uses Stata's percentile
cutpoints and keeps tied values together; ties can leave some groups empty.
`stata_recode()` follows Stata's `recode`: `1:5` is the range from 1 to 5,
including decimals, and values that no rule matches are kept.
